claims.claim: Velodyne HDL-64E cost around $75,000 and weighed 12.7 kg when used in the 2007 DARPA Urban Challenge.
claims.episode_span: David Hall’s Velodyne HDL-64E spun sixty four lasers on a roof rack and sold for roughly seventy five thousand dollars when five of the six finishers in the 2007 DARPA Urban Challenge used it.
claims.supporting_quote: In the 2007 DARPA Urban Challenge, five of the six teams that finished used lidar, and most of them used Velodyne’s HDL-64E. That sensor cost around $75,000. It spun 64 lasers to capture about 2.2 million points per second, and weighed 12.7 kg without cabling.

claims.claim: High-volume automotive lidar units reached roughly $200 in 2025 once monthly production passed 100,000 sensors.
claims.episode_span: High-volume units such as Hesai’s ATX reached roughly two hundred dollars in 2025 once the lasers, receivers, and drivers moved in-house and monthly production passed one hundred thousand sensors.
claims.supporting_quote: reached a run rate of 100,000 units a month in December 2024

claims.claim: The industry has converged on VCSEL arrays because thousands of emitters can be tested and binned on the same substrate.
claims.episode_span: Nature Communications notes that the industry converged on VCSEL arrays because they allow thousands of emitters to be tested and binned on the same substrate before any mechanical packaging.
claims.source_title: Evolution of laser technology for automotive LiDAR, an industrial viewpoint
claims.supporting_quote: recent trends suggest a growing convergence on vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (VCSEL) and antireflective VCSEL (AR-VCSEL) based solutions.
